links.note: 35 defines அறம் as what proceeds without slipping into four things, with அழுக்காறு named first. 161 takes that first item and tells a person to hold a heart without envy (அழுக்காறு இலாத இயல்பு) as his own ஒழுக்காறு, rule of conduct. Together they show envy treated as a matter of conduct to be kept, and not only as a feeling.

135 pairs the same two words: as the envious have no ஆக்கம், so one without ஒழுக்கம் has no உயர்வு. 161 fuses them, asking that freedom from அழுக்காறு be taken as ஒழுக்காறு. The rhyme ஒழுக்கு/அழுக்காறு is used in both to set envy and conduct side by side.

162 says that among excellent gains (விழுப்பேற்றின்) nothing equals being free of envy toward anyone (அஃதொப்பது இல்லை). 363 says there is no excellent wealth (விழுச்செல்வம்) like வேண்டாமை, here or there (அஃதொப்பது இல்). The same formula ranks an absence, of envy in the householder book and of wanting in the ascetic book, above every positive possession.

61 says that of all that can be gained (பெறுமவற்றுள்) the speaker knows none like children who know what should be known (மக்கட்பேறு). 162 uses the same vocabulary of பேறு for a gain that is purely inward: அழுக்காற்றின் அன்மை. Read together they show the book using 'the best of gains' for different goods in different chapters, so neither superlative should be taken as an exclusive ranking.

163 says the one who does not cherish another's prosperity (பிறனாக்கம் பேணாது) and envies it is called one who wants neither அறன் nor ஆக்கம். 1079 shows the same reaction in the கீழ்: on seeing others clothed and fed (உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம் காணின்) he is quick to find a fault in them. The later verse gives the behaviour that the earlier one judges.

141 says the folly of desiring a woman who is another's (பிறன்பொருளாள்) is not found in those who have seen அறம் and பொருள். 163 says the envier of பிறனாக்கம் is one who wants neither அறன் nor ஆக்கம். In adjacent chapters a wrong attitude to what is another's is measured against the same pair, virtue and wealth.

The second line of 136 is almost the second line of 164: இழுக்கத்தின் ஏதம் படுபாக்கு அறிந்து against இழுக்காற்றின் ஏதம் படுபாக்கு அறிந்து. In 136 the strong (உரவோர்) do not slacken in ஒழுக்கம்; in 164 people do no wrong out of envy (அழுக்காற்றின் அல்லவை செய்யார்). The repeated line gives the same ground for both restraints: knowing the harm that follows a lapse.

165 says envy is enough for the envious: it brings ruin even when enemies fail (ஒன்னார் வழுக்கியும் கேடீன்பது). 448 says a king without people who rebuke him perishes even with no one to ruin him (கெடுப்பார் இலானும் கெடும்). Both describe ruin that needs no outside enemy, once in a private vice and once in a ruler's unguarded state.

434 says fault itself is the enemy that brings one's end (குற்றமே அற்றம் தரூஉம் பகை). 165 says the same of one fault: envy suffices to ruin its holder without any ஒன்னார். The king's general rule in Book 2 has a specific case already stated in Book 1.

304 asks whether there is any other enemy than anger (சினத்தின் பகையும் உளவோ பிற), which kills smile and joy. 165 says the envious need no enemy since envy itself brings ruin. Two of the four things 35 excludes from virtue, anger and envy, are each described as the person's own enemy.

Both verses use the phrase உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம். In 1079 the base man sees others' clothing and food and finds fault with them; in 166 the kin of one who envies what is given (கொடுப்பது அழுக்கறுப்பான்) perish without clothing or food. The pairing shows what is envied returning as what is lost.

527 says crows do not hide food but call the others and eat, and that ஆக்கம் belongs only to those of that nature (அன்ன நீரார்க்கே). 166 gives the opposite disposition and result: one who grudges giving leaves his சுற்றம் without food or clothing. Both tie a household's kin and its prosperity to the attitude taken toward sharing.

167 says the fair goddess (செய்யவள்) grudges the envious man and shows him to her elder sister (தவ்வை). 617 names both sisters by residence: மாமுகடி lives in sloth, and தாமரையினாள் in the effort of the unslothful. The same pair of goddesses marks envy in Book 1 and sloth in Book 2 as conditions that hand a person over from fortune to misfortune.

84 says செய்யாள் dwells with a glad heart (அகனமர்ந்து) in the home of one who tends guests with a glad face. 167 has the same goddess grudge (அவ்வித்து) the envious man and pass him to her elder sister. She stays with the one who is glad to give to others and leaves the one who resents their good.

168 calls envy அழுக்காறு என ஒரு பாவி, which destroys fortune (திரு) and drives one to the bad place (தீயுழி). 1042 uses the same construction for poverty, இன்மை என ஒரு பாவி, which comes with both the next world and this one lost. Parimelazhagar reads 168 as a loss in both worlds too, so the two personified 'sinners' are given the same double effect.

169 says the prosperity of the crooked-hearted (அவ்விய நெஞ்சத்தான் ஆக்கம்) and the ruin of the upright (செவ்வியான் கேடு) will be pondered, which treats them as things that occur. 170 says none have grown great by envying (அழுக்கற்று அகன்றாரும் இல்லை) and none free of it have lost increase. The conflict holds if 169 is read as admitting real cases; Parimelazhagar removes it by supplying 'if they exist' and having the wise look for another cause.

117 says the world will not set down as ruin (கெடுவாக வையாது) the low state of one who stays in what is right through fairness. 169 lists the ruin of the upright (செவ்வியான் கேடு) as something to be pondered. 117 limits how that கேடு should be counted: the upright person's decline is not regarded as real ruin.

375 says that in making wealth good things can all turn bad and bad things good (நல்லவை எல்லாஅந் தீயவாம் தீயவும் நல்லவாம்), in the chapter on ஊழ். 169 leaves the envious man's prosperity and the upright man's ruin as a puzzle to be thought about (நினைக்கப்படும்). The fate chapter supplies one answer the book offers to that puzzle; Parimelazhagar's note on 169 likewise points to earlier deeds.

135 takes it as given that there is no ஆக்கம் in the envious (அழுக்காறுடையான்கண் ஆக்கம் ... இல்லை) and uses that as the comparison for conduct. 170 states the same as a rule with no exceptions: none have grown great through envy, and none without it have fallen away from பெருக்கம். The chapter on conduct relies on what the chapter on envy concludes.

171 says that coveting another's goods without fairness makes the family perish and brings faults at once (குடிபொன்றிக் குற்றமும் ஆங்கே தரும்). 604 says of the slothful that the family dies down and faults multiply (குடிமடிந்து குற்றம் பெருகும்). The same double penalty, on the குடி and in குற்றம், is attached to greed in Book 1 and to sloth in Book 2.

112 says the wealth of one who has rectitude (செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கம்) does not decay and is a security for his descendants (எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு). 171 gives the reverse case: coveting நடுவின்றி destroys the குடி. Both measure fairness about property by what happens to the family line and not only to the person.

172 says those ashamed of unfairness (நடுவன்மை நாணுபவர்) will not do blameworthy things out of desire for the gain to be had (படுபயன் வெஃகி). 113 gives the instruction that goes with it: gain that comes from leaving fairness (நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கம்) is to be dropped that very day, even if it brings only good. 172 describes the character and 113 the rule it follows.

164 says people do no wrong out of envy because they know the harm that comes of the wrong path (ஏதம் படுபாக்கு அறிந்து). 172 says people do nothing blameworthy out of coveting because they are ashamed of unfairness (நாணுபவர்). The neighbouring chapters use the same sentence shape, ending in செய்யார், with knowledge of consequences as the check in one and shame in the other.

173 says those who want the other joy (மற்றின்பம்) will not do what is not அறன் out of desire for a small joy (சிற்றின்பம்). 39 says only what comes through virtue is joy (அறத்தான் வருவதே இன்பம்) and all else lies outside it. 39 supplies the content of 173's 'other joy', and Parimelazhagar glosses it that way, as the lasting joy that comes by virtue; Pope instead takes it as the joy of heaven.

754 says wealth that comes without wrong and with knowledge of the means (தீதின்றி வந்த பொருள்) yields both அறன் and இன்பம். 173 says the small joy got by coveting is refused by those who want the other joy. Together they show the choice in 173 is not between wealth and joy: wealth rightly got delivers the joy that coveting forfeits.

174 says those of faultless sight who have conquered the senses will not covet on the thought 'we have nothing' (இலமென்று வெஃகுதல் செய்யார்). 205 forbids doing evil on the same plea (இலன் என்று தீயவை செய்யற்க) and adds that doing so makes one poor again. Both name poverty as the excuse and reject it; 205 gives the consequence that 174 leaves unstated.

1040 says the good woman called Land laughs on seeing those who sit idle saying 'we have nothing' (இலமென்று அசைஇ இருப்பாரை). 174 has the same words, இலமென்று, as the thought that does not move the self-controlled to covet. The plea of having nothing is refused twice: it excuses neither taking from others nor sitting idle.

656 says that even if one must see the mother who bore one go hungry (ஈன்றாள் பசி காண்பான் ஆயினும்), one should not do what the worthy condemn. 174 says the thought of being without does not make the self-controlled covet. 656 pushes the same refusal to its hardest case, where the want is another's and not one's own.

175 asks what fine and wide understanding comes to (அஃகி அகன்ற அறிவு என்னாம்) if one covets and acts senselessly toward everyone. 315 asks whether anything comes of understanding (அறிவினான் ஆகுவதுண்டோ) if one does not guard against another's pain as one's own. Both test அறிவு by how its owner treats other people, in coveting and in causing hurt.

834 says no one is a greater fool than the person who has studied, understood and taught others and yet does not restrain himself (தானடங்கா). 175 says subtle and wide understanding is worth nothing if its owner covets and does வெறிய things. Both hold that learning which does not govern conduct does not count.

285 says a loving nature with அருள் in view (அருள்கருதி) is not found in those who, with goods in view (பொருள்கருதி), watch for another's lapse. 176 says one who stands on the path desiring அருள் (அருள்வெஃகி) perishes if he desires பொருள் (பொருள்வெஃகி) and plots wrongs. Both verses set அருள் and பொருள் as rival objects of one desire and say the second drives out the first.

204 says not to plot another's ruin even by a lapse (சூழற்க), because அறம் will plot the ruin of the plotter (அறஞ்சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு). 176 says that one who plots wrongs for wealth (பொல்லாத சூழ) will perish (கெடும்). The shared verb சூழ் places the ruin at the stage of planning, before any act; 204 names the agent of that ruin.

177 says not to want gain that comes by coveting, since at its ripening (விளைவயின்) the fruit is hard to make good. 284 says the love grown strong in stealth yields, at its ripening (விளைவின்கண்), a sorrow that does not die. Coveting in the householder book and theft in the ascetic book are both judged by the harvest image, where the gain looks sound until it ripens.

931 opens with the same prohibition, வேண்டற்க: do not want gambling even if you win, because the winnings are like the hook a fish has swallowed. 177 says வேண்டற்க of the gain got by coveting, whose fruit turns out badly. Both warn against a gain that is real at the moment of taking and harmful afterwards.

177 argues from the outcome: gain got by coveting does not turn out well when enjoyed. 113 says gain that comes from leaving fairness is to be given up that very day even if it brings only good (நன்றே தரினும்). 113 removes the dependence on outcome, so the prohibition would stand even where 177's prediction failed.

178 asks what keeps wealth from shrinking (அஃகாமை செல்வத்திற்கு யாதெனின்) and answers: not coveting what is in another's hand. 112 says the wealth of one who has rectitude does not decay (சிதைவின்றி) and protects his descendants. Both make fairness about others' property the condition for one's own wealth lasting.

283 says gain made by stealth perishes beyond measure even as it seems to grow (ஆவது போலக் கெடும்). 178 says the way to keep wealth from shrinking is not to covet another's goods. 283 gives the negative side of the same claim: what is added by taking another's property is not a lasting addition.

179 says திரு, knowing the way (திறன் அறிந்து), goes to those who know virtue and do not covet. 594 says ஆக்கம் asks the way (அதர்வினாய்) and goes to the one of unwavering drive. In both, fortune is a traveller that seeks the person out; Book 1 gives non-coveting as what draws it and Book 2 gives energy.

130 says அறம் itself watches for the right moment (செவ்வி) and enters by the path of one who has guarded against anger and learned restraint. 179 says திரு knows the fitting way and reaches the one who does not covet. Each has a personified good coming unsought to a person defined by a restraint.

167 says the fair goddess grudges the envious man and shows him to her elder sister. 179 says திரு goes to those who know virtue and do not covet. The two neighbouring chapters use the goddess in opposite directions: she leaves the one who resents others' goods and comes to the one who does not want them.

180 says the pride called not-wanting (வேண்டாமை என்னுஞ் செருக்கு) yields victory, where Parimelazhagar glosses செருக்கு as wealth. 363 says there is no excellent wealth like வேண்டாமை in this world or the other. The word moves from not wanting another's goods in the householder chapter to not wanting anything in the renunciation chapter, and is counted a possession in both.

692 says that not desiring what kings desire (மன்னர் விழைப விழையாமை) brings lasting prosperity through those kings. 180 says not wanting others' goods yields victory, while coveting without thought yields destruction. The courtier's rule in Book 2 follows the same logic as 180: refraining from what belongs to another is what secures gain.
